overview: Arma families descended from soldiers who remained after Morocco invaded the Songhay Empire in 1591. Their locally rooted garrisons and pashas, or governors, became increasingly independent. This map shows a late slice, 1715 to 1783, of a much longer history around Timbuktu and the Niger River.

periods.title: From occupying army to local rulers
periods.summary: Moroccan garrisons developed local roots; by about 1660 their autonomy was established.

periods.title: Contested authority
periods.summary: Tuareg attacks, temporary recoveries and shifting alliances steadily reduced the pashalik’s power.

items.text: The name Arma is associated with an Arabic word for musketeers. Yet their story soon became about households as well as armies: descendants of the invaders established families and communities in the Niger towns, rather than remaining a temporary force sent from Morocco.

Garrisons occupied river towns between Kukya and Jenne. Their commanders collected tribute and supervised navigation. Control of a river landing mattered because merchants, supplies and tax payments moved through it: government depended on boats and trading towns as well as soldiers.

Old military divisions associated with Fez and Marrakesh became lasting family groups. Names such as Fasi and Marrakshi preserved memories of these origins even as the communities became part of local society. A surname could carry a much longer journey than its owner.

A Timbuktu library manuscript copied in 1733 charts the stars and connects their movements with seasons. Its astronomy also includes astrological ideas. The diagram offers a concrete glimpse of what a scholar might study during this map period.

An eighteenth-century arithmetic commentary by al-Rasmuki explains addition, subtraction, multiplication and division with charts. Books used in Timbuktu and North Africa made calculation a teachable skill. Even among desert manuscripts, somebody still had to do the sums.

A poem by al-Mukhtar al-Kunti discusses the rights of orphans and married women. Verse helped readers remember legal instruction. Another manuscript treats contracts and loans in verse: rhyme could help carry serious rules about money and responsibility.

A medical manuscript from the same library collection describes illnesses, plant, animal and mineral preparations, and prayers or protective amulets. It records historical approaches to healing, rather than advice to follow today. These collections preserve the city’s wider scholarly life, not only Arma authors.

A small Arabic sample is “الباب الاول”, meaning “the first chapter”, from the 1898 printed edition of al-Sadi’s seventeenth-century history of the region. Arabic was a language of historical scholarship. This is a later printed witness, not a surviving page in the author’s own handwriting.

Timbuktu’s Djingareyber, Sankore and Sidi Yahia mosques are older than the Arma map interval. Their earthen architecture depended on repeated care. UNESCO emphasizes surviving construction techniques and maintenance: keeping a famous building standing is itself a skilled, continuing achievement.

Timbuktu was never simply a military headquarters. Its scholars and prominent families maintained institutions of learning and asserted local autonomy under successive rulers. Their influence helps explain why a change of soldiers did not automatically replace the city’s intellectual and civic life.

The Kel Tadamakkat defeated the pashalik in 1737, but Arma authority briefly recovered after 1755. Further attacks followed. Historian Ariela Marcus-Sells places the decisive Iwellemmedan capture of Timbuktu in 1787, illustrating a long erosion of power rather than a single neat collapse in the map’s last year.

Arma communities continued after the pashalik. In a February 2023 justice meeting, an Arma community leader from Gao described helping settle minor land and family disputes and referring larger matters to formal courts. This is a dated modern example of community life, not a claim that eighteenth-century government survives unchanged.

ending.text: Arma political supremacy weakened through eighteenth-century warfare; the 1787 capture of Timbuktu is one scholarly endpoint for the pashalik. The map’s 1783 cutoff is not an established fall date. Arma families and communities continued.
